case.title: Thornley Reach: who pays for the failed housing company?
case.question: How should Thornley Reach cover the £43m lost on its failed council housing company?
case.story: Thornley Reach is a made-up borough of 180,000 people. Eight years ago the council set up its own housing company, Thornley Homes, and lent it £74m to build 620 homes. 410 are built or half-built, and the council can sell them for about £31m, which leaves a £43m hole. The council has £8m in reserves, its yearly budget is already cut to the bone, and it must balance its books by law. A council tax rise within the limit that needs no local vote brings in £5m a year. Every route hurts someone, and the council meets on Wednesday to choose.

in_the_news.headline: Lambeth Greens declare financial emergency over Homes for Lambeth
in_the_news.why: Lambeth's council says it must write off £60m to £68m on its housing company and asked government for help; Thornley Reach is a made-up council facing the same kind of hole.

facts.text: Lambeth Council estimates it will have to write off between £60m and £68m over its housing company, Homes for Lambeth.
Lambeth also faces £143m of cuts and a budget gap over the next three years.
The housing ministry said tenants in Lambeth council homes will not have to pay for losses or debts from council-owned companies.

sources.title: Lambeth Greens declare financial emergency over Homes for Lambeth
Exceptional Financial Support for local authorities for 2026-27

tests.text: The books balance this year and next, as the law requires. No borrowing to paper over it.
No council tenant loses their home or pays for the company’s debt.
No cut to adult social care or children’s services.
No council tax rise above the limit that needs no local vote.
Residents are told in plain words what was lost and who decided to lend the money.
The 410 homes are finished or sold within two years, with a named builder or buyer.

voices.text: I live in a council flat. If they sell flats to pay for a company I was never asked about, I want that said out loud before the vote, not after.
Four hundred homes half-built and nobody at the council will say who signed for the loan. Give us the name, then give us the bill.

voices.who: out of work, 53, Yorkshire and The Humber
voices.text: Don’t take the old folks’ care to pay for a building scheme. Find who ran it and make them answer for it.
I’d pay a bit more on the council tax if I could see where every pound went. Show me the homes, not a promise.

bench.angle: Sell council homes and sites to fill the gap
bench.title: Sell 350 council homes and spare sites to clear the debt
bench.answer: The council sells about 350 of its own homes and spare building sites, raising about £35m. With the £8m in reserves, that covers the £35m left after the 410 company homes are sold. The cabinet decides; the finance director signs the sale list and publishes it before Wednesday's vote. The council pays, out of its own housing stock. The tenants in those homes lose them, though the council offers them other council homes first. No tax rise and no care cuts. We would know it worked if the books balance this year and next, the sales raise £35m or more, and the gap is closed without new borrowing.

bench.angle: Cut services and raise tax to the limit over years
bench.title: Raise council tax to the limit and cut services over three years
bench.answer: The council raises council tax by the most it can without a local vote, bringing in £5m a year, and cuts £7m a year from other services, including adult social care, for three years. Together with the £8m in reserves, that covers the gap by the third year. The cabinet decides and the finance director signs each year's cuts, published in full. Council taxpayers and people who use those services pay. No council homes are sold. We would know it worked if the debt is cleared in three years, each year's cuts match the published list, and no new borrowing is needed.

bench.angle: Wind the company down and ask government for help
bench.title: Close the company; ask government to cover the gap
bench.answer: The council winds the company down, stops new lending and sells its 410 homes within two years, publishing the buyer before signing. Protect existing council tenants, rents, care and children’s services. Use the expected £31m sale proceeds and £8m reserves; request a £35m government grant, paid by national taxpayers. The council’s finance director publishes who authorised the £74m loan and quarterly accounts showing receipts, the remaining gap and homes sold. Success means all 410 sold and balanced books this year and next without new borrowing. Until government agrees and the money arrives, the books do not balance. A begging letter is not £35m.

rows.note: The sums close: £35m of sales plus £8m reserves covers the £43m hole, with no tax rise and no new borrowing; it gives no dates for when the cash lands.
Tenants in the 350 homes sold lose them; the offer of other council homes comes first but is only an offer, so tenants do lose their homes.
It says outright there are no care cuts, and nothing in it touches adult social care or children’s services.
It says there is no tax rise, so council tax stays at or below the no-vote limit.
It publishes the sale list before the vote but says nothing on telling residents what was lost or who decided to lend the £74m.
It assumes the 410 company homes are sold but gives no two-year deadline and names no builder or buyer.
The £5m tax plus £7m cuts add up to the gap over three years, but it says nothing on how this year and next balance before the debt is cleared.
No homes are sold, but council taxpayers pay, and council tenants who pay council tax are among them, so tenants help pay the company’s debt.
It cuts £7m a year from other services, naming adult social care, for three years.
The rise is set at the most the council can make without a local vote, so it stays within the limit.
Each year’s cuts are published in full, but it says nothing on telling residents what was lost or who decided to lend.
It is silent on the 410 homes: no sale or finish date and no named builder or buyer.
The £35m grant is only requested, and it says the books do not balance until government agrees and the money arrives.
It protects existing council tenants and rents and sells only the company’s homes, so no tenant loses a home or pays the debt.
It names care and children’s services as protected.
It pays from sale proceeds, reserves and a grant, and proposes no council tax rise.
The finance director publishes who authorised the £74m loan, with quarterly accounts showing receipts and the remaining gap.
It sells all 410 homes within two years and publishes the buyer before signing.

gate.verdict: Answer A keeps care, tax and the books inside their limits but sells tenants’ homes; B cuts adult social care and makes taxpayers, tenants included, pay; C protects everyone but leaves the books unbalanced until a grant arrives.

jury.question: Which red line, if any, should the town be asked to rethink?
options: Council tenants’ homes: sell some council homes to close the gap
Care: cut adult social care and children’s services for three years
Balanced books: borrow to cover the gap until a government grant arrives
None: keep every red line and keep looking for a route that breaks none
jury.ruling: Keep every red line, 6 to 4 over selling council homes, with 1 for cutting care and 1 for borrowing.

reasons.text: Sell some stock. The books have to balance, and tenants are offered other council homes first.
Care is what we need at my age. Sell what the council owns, not what keeps us going.
Not my flat. If something has to give, let the services take the cut before the tenants lose their homes.
Don’t touch the old folks’ care. If they’re going to sell anything, they can tell us what first.

minister.text: Nothing is signed. Every answer crossed a red line: A sells tenants’ homes, B cuts adult social care, C leaves the books unbalanced until a grant arrives. The £43m goes back to the council.
minister.statement: I’m sending this back. A sells tenants’ homes. B cuts adult social care and makes tenants pay too. C protects everyone, but the books don’t balance until a grant turns up, and a begging letter isn’t £35m. Twelve citizens said keep every red line, 6 to 4 over selling council homes. I agree. Nobody should lose their keys to pay for a company they never voted on. Bring back a plan that breaks none, and name who signed the loan.
